desc:
A zigzag path is built like this: pick any starting node and an initial direction, left or right. Move to the child in that direction if it exists, then switch direction (left becomes right and right becomes left) and repeat. The walk stops when the child in the required direction is missing. A single node is a zigzag path of length 0.

Return the length, in edges, of the longest zigzag path of the tree. The node values do not matter for this problem; only the shape counts. The empty tree gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, -1, 4, -1, -1, 5] the answer is 3: start at the root, go left to 2, right to 4 and left to 5.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: From a node, a zigzag walk has only two possibilities for its first move: left or right. After that, the whole walk is forced.
Define two numbers per node: the longest zigzag that starts at this node and goes left first, and the one that goes right first. Express each with the child's values.
L[v] = 1 + R[left child] if the left child exists (else 0), and R[v] = 1 + L[right child] if the right child exists (else 0). The answer is the largest L or R over all nodes.
editorial: After the first move the path is forced: it always has to continue in the opposite direction. So a zigzag walk starting at v and first going left consists of the edge to the left child a, followed by a zigzag walk that starts at a and goes right first. That yields the recurrences L[v] = 1 + R[a] and R[v] = 1 + L[b] for the right child b, with the value 0 when the child is missing.

Any zigzag path starts somewhere, so the answer is the maximum of all L[v] and R[v]. Computing the values from the last real node to the first one makes sure the children are ready (a child always sits after its parent in level order). Trying every start with a fresh simulation would also work but is O(n · depth) in the worst case.
